result.topic_en: Euler asks whether the interpolating curve through the points of the sine line really is the sine curve. He reduces this to an identity between products of Beta-type integrals, checks it for n = 1/4 and ω = 1/2, and then states it as a theorem (§44) and begins the proof.
result.transcription:
196
vt sit $f = \sin. n\pi$, et puncta omnia data in linea sinuum sint sita. Hinc autem non sequitur ipsam curuam, quam aequatio inuenta exhibet, esse lineam sinuum, cum innumerabiles aliae curuae per eadem puncta data transire queant. Quare neutiquam etiamnunc certum est, valorem ipsius $y$, abscissae $x = \omega\pi$ conuenientem, et hac aequatione definitum:
$\frac{n\Delta y}{(n-\omega)\sin.n\pi} = \frac{\pi\omega f.n\pi.\sin.\omega\pi}{\sin.(n-\omega)\pi.\sin.(n+\omega)\pi}$,
aequari sinui arcus $\pi\omega$, vt sit $y = \sin.\pi\omega$, etiamsi hoc verum sit casibus $\omega = \pm(1 \pm n)$ et $\omega = 0$. Supra quidem vidimus, casu etiam, quo $\omega$ est quantitas minima, aequationem fore veritati consentaneam, sumendo $y = \sin.\pi\omega$, ita vt sit $\Delta = \frac{\pi\omega}{\sin.n\pi}$, existente:
$\Delta = \frac{\int z^{n-1}dz(1-z)^{-n}\int z^{n-1}dz(1-z)^{n}}{\int z^{n-1}dz(1-z)^{-2n}}$,
quemadmodum etiam ibi demonstraui. Quo autem haec res facilius in genere explorari possit, pro valore $\Delta$ commodius exprimendo obseruo esse:
$\frac{\int z^{n+\omega-1}dz(1-z)^{-n-\omega}}{\int z^{n+\omega-1}dz(1-z)^{-2n}} = \frac{\int z^{\omega-n}dz(1-z)^{-n-\omega}}{\int dz(1-z)^{-2n}}$
$=(1-2n)\int z^{\omega-n}dz(1-z)^{-n-\omega}$,
dum sit $n < \frac{1}{2}$, vnde erit:
$\Delta = (1-2n)\int z^{\omega-n}dz(1-z)^{-n-\omega}\int z^{n+\omega-1}dz(1-z)^{n-\omega}$.
Verum si esset in genere $y = \sin.\omega\pi$, foret
$\Delta = \frac{(n-\omega)\pi\sin.n\pi\cos.n\pi}{n\sin.(n-\omega)\pi.\sin.(n+\omega)\pi}$.
Quaestio ergo huc redit: vtrum haec aequatio:
$(1-2n)\int z^{\omega-n}dz(1-z)^{-n-\omega}\cdot\int z^{n+\omega-1}dz(1-z)^{n-\omega}$
$=\frac{(n-\omega)\pi\sin.n\pi\cos.n\pi}{n\sin.(n-\omega)\pi.\sin.(n+\omega)\pi}$,
etiam

197
etiam aliis casibus, praeter supra memoratos, sit vera, nec ne? Hunc in finem consideremus casum, quo $n = \frac{1}{4}$ et $\omega = \frac{1}{2}$, vbi posterior quidem pars fit
$=\frac{-\frac{1}{4}\pi.\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}}.\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}}}{-\frac{1}{4}\cdot\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}}\cdot\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}}} = \pi$;
prior vero pars erit
$=\frac{1}{2}\int\frac{z^{\frac{1}{4}}dz}{(1-z)^{\frac{3}{4}}}\cdot\int\frac{z^{-\frac{1}{4}}dz}{(1-z)^{\frac{1}{4}}}$
quae posito $z = v^4$ abit in hanc formam:
$8\int\frac{v^4dv}{\sqrt[4]{(1-v^4)^3}}\cdot\int\frac{v^2dv}{\sqrt[4]{(1-v^4)}} = 4\int\frac{dv}{\sqrt[4]{(1-v^4)^3}}\cdot\int\frac{vvdv}{\sqrt[4]{(1-v^4)}}$
cuius valor per ea, quae circa huiusmodi formulas demonstraui, reuera fit $= \pi$, quod ergo iam est documentum insigne pro veritate nostrae aequationis, quam autem sequenti modo perfecte demonstrare licet.
Theorema.
§. 44. Quomodocunque bini numeri $n$ et $\omega$ accipiantur, haec aequatio veritati erit consentanea:
$(1-2n)\int\frac{z^{\omega-n}dz}{(1-z)^{n+\omega}}\cdot\int\frac{z^{n+\omega-1}dz}{(1-z)^{\omega-n}} = \frac{(n-\omega)\pi\sin.n\pi.\cos.n\pi}{n\sin.(n-\omega)\pi.\sin.(n+\omega)\pi}$,
si quidem illarum formularum integratio a termino $z = 0$ ad terminum $z = 1$ extendatur.
Demonstratio.
Quo has formulas integrales ad formam, quam tractaui, reducamus, ponamus $n + \omega = \frac{\mu}{\lambda}$ et $\omega - n = \frac{\nu}{\lambda}$,
Bb 3          vt

items.quote: Quare neutiquam etiamnunc certum est, valorem ipsius $y$, abscissae $x = \omega\pi$ conuenientem, et hac aequatione definitum: ... aequari sinui arcus $\pi\omega$, vt sit $y = \sin.\pi\omega$
items.english: Therefore it is by no means yet certain that the value of y corresponding to the abscissa x = ωπ, and defined by this equation, equals the sine of the arc πω, so that y = sin πω.

items.quote: Quaestio ergo huc redit: vtrum haec aequatio: ... etiam aliis casibus, praeter supra memoratos, sit vera, nec ne?
items.english: The question therefore comes down to this: whether this equation is also true in other cases besides those mentioned above, or not?

items.quote: cuius valor per ea, quae circa huiusmodi formulas demonstraui, reuera fit $= \pi$
items.english: Its value, by what I have demonstrated about formulas of this kind, really is π.

items.quote: Quomodocunque bini numeri $n$ et $\omega$ accipiantur, haec aequatio veritati erit consentanea: ... si quidem illarum formularum integratio a termino $z = 0$ ad terminum $z = 1$ extendatur.
items.english: However the two numbers n and ω are taken, this equation will agree with the truth, provided the integration of those formulas is extended from z = 0 to z = 1.
